intro: Most people who know the Bible know Genesis from a distance: a garden, a snake, a flood, a coat of many colors. This unit reads it up close. You will open the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation to Genesis 1, 2, 3 and 22, and then to the long stories of Jacob and Joseph in chapters 25 to 50, and read them the way a careful reader reads anything: slowly, noticing what the words say, what they repeat and what they leave out.

You will not read alone. At the table will be the classical Jewish commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban, the rabbis of the midrash, and modern readers from a German philologist writing in exile to an American literary critic. You will meet the Babylonian creation poem that was dug out of the ground in the 1800s and the academic theory that sees several sources woven into the Torah. Each reader asks different questions, and this unit teaches you to say whose question you are asking.

By the end you will be able to describe the structure of a passage, show how a repeated word or a silence carries meaning, compare two commentators on one verse, and explain how Jewish and Christian traditions read the same chapter differently, all without deciding for anyone what the text must mean. That is close reading, and it is the skill this course builds on from here.
bigQuestion: What does a reader see in Genesis when the words are read slowly, with the text's oldest and newest readers side by side?

timeline.t: Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation poem, is in circulation in Mesopotamia by about this time
The Babylonian exile; many scholars date the shaping of Genesis in its present form to around this period
Greek translation of the Torah, the Septuagint, begins in Alexandria
Genesis Rabbah, the major rabbinic midrash on Genesis, is compiled in the land of Israel
The Aleppo Codex, a model Masoretic Bible manuscript, is written
Rashi, in Troyes, France, writes the commentary that Jewish study still starts from
Ramban writes his Torah commentary, often arguing with Rashi and Ibn Ezra
Kierkegaard publishes Fear and Trembling, a Christian philosopher's reading of the Akedah
George Smith publishes the Babylonian creation account from tablets found at Nineveh
Wellhausen's Prolegomena gives the documentary hypothesis its classic form
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh, the text this course reads
Robert Alter's The Art of Biblical Narrative describes the Bible's literary techniques

words.d: "In the beginning," the first word of the Torah and the Hebrew name of Genesis
a line repeated at set points, such as the evening-and-morning line in Genesis 1
verse-by-verse explanation printed beside the text, such as Rashi's
rabbinic interpretation that fills a text's gaps with story, law or teaching
the plain sense of a text in its grammar and context
the academic theory that the Torah was woven from several sources, labeled J, E, D and P
the Binding of Isaac, Genesis 22, read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah
what a story leaves out, which readers and interpreters may fill
a repeated word that links scenes and carries meaning; Buber and Rosenzweig's Leitwort
a set narrative pattern, like the meeting at a well, retold with telling variations
return or repentance; fully, meeting the same situation and choosing differently
a weekly Torah portion read on Shabbat; Genesis has twelve

test.q: Which name for God is used throughout Genesis 1:1–2:3?
test.why: The first creation account uses Elohim from start to finish; "the LORD God" begins at Genesis 2:4.

test.q: Which commentator opens on Genesis 1:1 by asking why the Torah does not begin with the first commandment?
test.why: Rashi's first comment asks why a book of commandments starts with creation and answers that the earth is God's to give.

test.q: What happens to Tiamat in Enuma Elish?
choices: Marduk kills her and makes sky and earth from her body
test.why: The Babylonian poem has creation follow a battle; Genesis 1 has creation by speech with no rival.

test.q: In Genesis 2, what is created last?
test.why: Genesis 2 forms the man, plants the garden, forms the animals and last builds the woman; Genesis 1 makes male and female together, last.

test.q: How does Rashi explain God's question "Where art thou?" in Genesis 3:9?
choices: God asked gently so the man would not be frightened and could answer
God did not know where the man was
The question was addressed to the serpent
The question is a scribe's addition
test.why: Rashi, following midrash, says God knew and opened with a question to start a conversation without fear.

test.q: Which doctrine belongs to Christian tradition, through Augustine, and not to mainstream Jewish reading of Genesis 3?
test.why: Original sin, an inherited fallen state, is Augustine's teaching; the two inclinations, seventy faces and measure for measure are rabbinic ideas.

test.q: Under the documentary hypothesis, which source is the garden story of Genesis 2–3 assigned to?
test.why: The garden story, with the LORD God and its vivid dialogue, is assigned to J; Genesis 1 is assigned to P.

test.q: Which of these did Solomon Schechter do in 1903?
test.why: Schechter's address objected to the low view of Judaism in some leading critics; the other events belong to 1917, 1876 and 1843.

test.q: Which line is repeated in Genesis 22 before and after Isaac's only question?
choices: "And they went both of them together"
test.why: The walking-together line frames the exchange between father and son in verses 6 and 8.

test.q: What did Erich Auerbach say about the style of Genesis 22 compared to Homer?
choices: Genesis describes everything in the foreground
Genesis leaves nearly everything unspoken, "fraught with background"
test.why: Mimesis (1946) opens with this contrast between Homer's fully lit scenes and the Bible's silence.

test.q: Why is a ram's horn sounded on Rosh Hashanah, according to Rabbi Abbahu in the Talmud?
choices: Because Moses sounded one at Sinai
Because rams were common in Babylon
So that God will remember the binding of Isaac
test.why: Rosh Hashanah 16a links the shofar to the ram of the Akedah and asks God to remember the binding on the people's behalf.

test.q: What did Buber and Rosenzweig call the repeated word that ties scenes together?
test.why: Leitwort, leading word or keyword, is their term; type-scene is Alter's, and peshat and parashah are different concepts.

test.q: Which detail in the Jacob story do many readers hear as an answer to his deception of Isaac?
choices: Laban gives him the elder sister in the dark
test.why: Jacob, who took the elder's place by deceiving a blind father, is deceived in the dark about which sister he married.

test.q: What is Judah's speech in Genesis 44:18–34 known for?
choices: Being the longest speech in Genesis and the story's turning point
Being the first mention of Benjamin
test.why: Judah's seventeen-verse plea, offering himself in place of Benjamin, moves Joseph to reveal himself.

test.q: What is the difference between reading Genesis as literature and as Torah, as this unit describes it?
choices: Literature is for Jews; Torah is for everyone
Only one of them uses Rashi
Reading as literature asks what the text does; reading as Torah asks what the text asks of the reader
test.why: The two approaches ask different questions and often share readers; the unit teaches students to say which one is speaking.

write.prompt: Does the narrator of Genesis judge the people in its stories, or leave judgment to the reader? Cite Genesis 25:34, Genesis 27:22 and Genesis 50:20, or another set of three passages from this unit. For each, say what the text states and what it withholds, and show how at least two readers (for example Rashi, Ramban, Genesis Rabbah, Alter or Auerbach) have handled it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you cite, and the translation you read it in.
Attribute every reading to its reader or tradition: "Rashi reads," "the midrash says," "Alter argues."
Describe how readers differ; do not rank traditions or say which reading is true.
Use the unit's terms where they fit: economy, gap, keyword, type-scene, peshat, midrash.
Keep your own view separate and clearly marked, and support it from the text's words.
